claim: sqlglot tokenizes an unquoted `TABLE` word (any case) as `TokenType.TABLE`, while a double-quoted/backquoted `"table"` tokenizes as an identifier token type, in every dialect the guard is used with and across sqlglot 30.22-30.31.

claim: `sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise(dialect)` raises `ValueError` (and nothing else) for an unrecognized dialect name, accepts `None`, and the returned object exposes a `tokenize(sql)` method that raises `sqlglot.errors.TokenError` for unterminated strings/comments.

The docstring asserts the tokenizer check flags a `TABLE` keyword exactly when it starts the SQL or follows `;`, `(`, `UNION`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`, `ALL` or `DISTINCT`, and that a quoted identifier never counts — i.e. no other position in which PostgreSQL/MySQL accept `TABLE t` exists.
source_excerpt:
A ``TABLE`` keyword token (an unquoted ``table`` in any case; a quoted
    identifier is not one) counts when it starts the SQL or follows ``;``,
    ``(``, ``UNION``, ``INTERSECT``, ``EXCEPT``, ``ALL`` or ``DISTINCT``.

claim: The module docstring asserts `TABLE t` is refused in any statement or subquery, found with the tokenizer, and that a `TABLE s.t` which does not parse is refused as unparseable SQL.
source_excerpt:
``TABLE t``, PostgreSQL's
and MySQL's shorthand for ``SELECT * FROM t``, is refused in any statement or
subquery. It is found with sqlglot's tokenizer (``uses_table_shorthand``),
because sqlglot parses it differently across versions (a name ``TABLE``
before 30.30, ``SELECT * FROM t`` from 30.30). A ``TABLE s.t`` that does not
parse is refused as unparseable SQL.
